summary: Iterative adversarial polish of the live-cart idea: 3 hostile judges score, a simplifier rewrites and cuts, repeat up to 3 rounds

objections: Every piece except one already exists. Round 1 of this project killed 'tap the item in your friend's live video and it's yours' at a 4 (Verishop Shop Party 2020: friends on video see each other's carts and add to their own; Instacart family accounts add items and approve swaps on a live order; TikTok Shop/Whatnot tap-to-buy). The auto-split is also shipped: Tab says 'multiple people can select the same item if they shared it', syncs it live, and Splitsy and Checkify split one item across several people with one tap. The only new part is doing that co-claim on a physical object in a live cart video, before checkout, with a hold per share. Judges will see Shop Party plus Tab unless the very first beat shows that moment.

The split has no reason to exist in the eggs example. Housemates who each want eggs want their own carton, not a third of one, so three-way co-claiming an ordinary item is rare and looks staged. The split only makes sense for packs nobody would buy alone (the Costco idea), and that ground is also taken: Bulkshare.ai, ClubSave/BulkBuySplitter and BulkSharely split Costco packs among neighbors, and Groupon's tipping point and Pinduoduo team buys already do 'buy only once fully committed'. The live, in-aisle version of that threshold is the only fresh angle.

The money path is half real. The shopper still pays the full amount at the register with their own card, so they front the money. A Cybersource hold-then-capture on a friend's card pays a merchant account, not the shopper, and getting money to the friend needs a P2P push (Visa Direct, which isn't on the available list) or Venmo (no API). Trust also takes a hit: a phone clipped to the cart streams continuously and films other shoppers and store staff to a group of viewers.
cut: Drag 2 (your cart into their feed to ping the shopper, plus shelf highlighting). This is the 'grab me something' errand already shipped by NeedAnything, Runerra, Buy4Me and OurGroceries, and round 2 banned it in any form. It also doubles the CV work: shelf search on top of tracking items in the cart.

Fridge-camera pre-fill and past-habit suggestions. Household inventory cameras are a graveyard (Samsung Family Hub, Smarter FridgeCam). It's a second camera and a second demo with no effect on the money moment.
The browser-agent online-order fallback. It's a separate product, the lessons say agent buying should be a small part, and it pulls judges away from the live cart.
A personal 'YOUR cart' as a persistent object. With drag 2 and the fridge pre-fill gone, a viewer only needs to claim and see their running share. A second cart UI is extra.
A continuous all-trip feed for everyone. Stream only while items are in view or claimable, which shrinks the privacy surface and the bandwidth.
Splitting ordinary single items (eggs). Keep splitting only where the pack is too big for one person, or drop the eggs example from the pitch.
verdicts.prior_art: I searched the web and the team's round 1 and 2 notes. Nobody ships the exact core: drag a physical item out of a live cart video, and when several viewers grab the same item it splits among them with a hold on each share before checkout. Each neighbor of it is shipped, though. (1) Live video plus friends adding items: Verishop Shop Party (Dec 2020, friends see each other's carts on video), Instacart family-account collaboration (add items, approve swaps on a live order), TikTok Shop, Whatnot, Facebook Live, Grocery Outlet shoppable livestreams. Round 1's prior-art hunter already killed this exact 'tap the Takis in your friend's video' framing at a 4. (2) Several people claiming one item and splitting it automatically: Tab ('multiple people can select the same item', real-time multi-phone join), Splitsy, Checkify, Splittz, SplitNow, Banana Splits, GrocerMate. All of these work from the receipt after purchase. (3) Splitting bulk packs: Bulkshare.ai, ClubSave/BulkBuySplitter, BulkSharely. Threshold-based buying: Groupon's tipping point, Pinduoduo team purchase. (4) Asking the shopper to grab something: NeedAnything, Runerra, Buy4Me, OurGroceries, Kando Errands (per-errand card). (5) CV carts: KARTX (Raspberry Pi cart camera tracking items added and removed), OpenMV smart-cart prototypes on Hackaday, and a LiveKit vision-in-stream product-card system on LinkedIn. Also 2026 winner EcoBite ('let your floor claim the rest in real time'), which is close on the social 'claim' verb. Novelty of the core: low to medium. It moves Tab's co-claim from the receipt to a live physical object and attaches a hold per share.
verdicts.best: The co-claim on a physical object. Two judges drag the same Kirkland pack from the live cart at once, a ring around it fills, and each card shows a hold for exactly their share. Once the ring is full, the pack becomes 'buy'. If it never fills, the holds void. I found no shipped app or Devpost project that does this live and before checkout, and it maps directly onto real sandbox Visa features (one auth hold per share, partial capture, void). Make the Costco bulk-share ring the whole product, not an optional add-on. It's the only version where splitting one item is something people actually want, and it gives the 10-second, two-person, camera-driven money moment the earlier rounds asked for.

objections: Nobody in my house watches a live cart feed. When Jake goes to QFC, the rest of us are in class, asleep, or gaming, and we text 'grab eggs' and look again when he's back. A continuous feed needs everyone watching at the same moment, which never happens on a real grocery run. The auto-split only works if the cart can be claimed later: the shopper snaps the cart (or the pack at Costco), everyone claims within the next ~20 minutes, and splits settle by themselves. As written, live viewing is the core of the app, and it's the part I'd never open unprompted.

The camera setup contradicts itself and the shopper takes on all the work. A phone clipped to the handle and pointed down at the cart can't see shelves, so drag #2 ('highlight it on the shelf') can't happen. Pointed forward, it can't see the cart, so drag #1 has nothing to show. The shopper also loses their phone for the whole trip (no list, no Maps, battery dying) and streams strangers in every aisle. The one person doing us a favor gets the worst experience, so nobody volunteers to shop.

The money path isn't explained. I put a hold on my card, it captures 'at handoff', and then how does Jake get paid? Captures settle to a merchant account. That means the app becomes the merchant and pays Jake out (money transmission), or it needs Visa Direct, which isn't on the 'genuinely runs' list. Venmo is explicitly ruled out. 'Handoff' also needs a trigger: who confirms the eggs reached me? Until this is one honest sentence, a judge who asks 'where does the $1.67 go?' sinks the Trust score. Holds that small on every claimer's card also clutter statements, and one decline breaks the split.
cut: Fridge camera pre-fill: no student owns a fridge camera, and it's a second vision pipeline unrelated to the money moment
'Past habits' suggestions: adds a recommendation system and nothing a judge can touch
Browser-agent fallback ordering: agent buying was supposed to be a small part, and this turns the app into two products. Drop it from the demo and mention it once at most

Drag #2 (push an item into the shopper's feed plus shelf highlighting): this is a text message. It needs a forward camera, Perceptron grounding on shelves, and push notifications, all for something the group chat already does

The continuous live video stream to every housemate: switch to a snapshot or short clip the shopper posts, which can still be claimed by drag. That removes the streaming infrastructure and fixes the camera-angle contradiction
'A share of it' as a general option on every item: limit splitting to items several people drag (and bulk packs). No custom-ratio UI

Keep the Costco bulk-share ring and make it the hero scenario rather than an option. A shared house splitting a 5 lb bag of rice or 48 eggs at Costco is the real use case, and 'only buy the pack once it's fully claimed' is the clearest visible link between what the camera sees and the money
verdicts.prior_art: This is closest to GrocerMate and Banana Split (receipt lines matched to the people who wanted them) and Splitwise and Tab (splitting), with NeedAnything, Runerra and Buy4Me for 'friends add requests to your run'. The live-feed tap-to-claim looks like TikTok Shop, Whatnot and Facebook Live with a housemate in place of the merchant, plus Verishop Shop Party for shopping together on video. Instacart's shopper photo chat already covers 'is this the right one?'. Kando Errands has per-errand cards but nothing to stop the shopper fronting the money. What's actually new is narrow: claims put a hold on each claimer's own card before checkout (so the shopper never fronts), the split forms by itself from who claimed, and bulk packs only get bought once fully claimed. The live video is not the new part, and it's the most-copied part.
verdicts.best: Auto-split by claiming. Three of us drag the same carton, it splits three ways, each of us has a hold on our own card, and the shopper never fronts a cent or chases anyone on Venmo. That fixes the most annoying thing about house runs (Jake fronting $140 and then begging for payback for two weeks). Put it on a Costco bulk pack whose ring fills as housemates claim shares, and a judge can drag a share in the first 10 seconds and watch the ring and their hold update. Everything else in the spec is optional; this is the product.

objections: Where does the captured money go? Each claimer's hold is captured to the app's Cybersource sandbox merchant account, but the shopper paid the store with their own card, and nothing on the available list pays the shopper back (no Visa Direct, no Venmo). A Visa judge will ask in the first minute. If you don't answer it on screen, the app looks like an unlicensed money transmitter with the last step faked. The fix is to say it out loud: the platform is merchant of record for the reimbursement, and the payout to the shopper is the one stubbed step (or use Visa Direct if you can actually get sandbox access). Hiding it loses more Trust points than admitting it.

There is no agent at the core, and the AI is the riskiest part to build. The core is 'drag a box off a live video'. That needs Perceptron to find and keep tracking items in a moving, cluttered cart at a frame rate that feels live. If the boxes lag 1 to 2 seconds or jump between items, the hero gesture breaks while the judge's finger is on it. Don't drag live boxes. Detect when an item is added to the cart, freeze it as a cropped thumbnail chip in a strip under the video, and let people drag the chip. The vision still matters (it decides what was added, reads the label for the name and estimated price, and later reads the receipt for the real price), and the gesture never depends on tracking.

Commerce Impact is thin for merchants. This is reimbursement among friends for a purchase that would have happened anyway, and Splitwise, Tab, GrocerMate and Banana Split already split receipts. Your only merchant story is basket uplift from people adding items remotely, and Expo judges will doubt that housemates actually watch a live cart feed. Lead with the auto-split as the new thing (holding the full price on each claim, then capturing only your share at the real receipt price), not with the 'live feed', which Instacart's photo chat and Verishop Shop Party already did.
cut: Drag #2 (send an item from your cart to the shopper's feed and highlight it on the shelf). It is NeedAnything, Runerra and Buy4Me plus shelf detection in a real store, which you cannot show at an expo table. It doubles the gesture model and adds nothing to the money moment.
Fridge camera pre-fill and past-habit suggestions. That is a second camera, a second vision pipeline and a second product (household inventory apps are a graveyard). It doesn't help the split demo.

The browser-agent fallback ('if nobody is shopping, the agent orders online'). It contradicts the lesson that agent buying should be a small part, and it puts the existing Gemini repo in the pitch for no points. Mention it in one sentence or not at all.

The Costco bulk ring as a separate feature. It is the same mechanic as auto-split with an extra 'not bought yet' state. Either drop it or make it the visual for auto-split: a ring around the chip that fills one segment per claimer.

Visa Token Service lifecycle, Trusted Agent Protocol, and mandate approval prompts. None of them is structurally needed here. Keep only auth hold on claim, partial capture of the share at handoff, and void if the item isn't bought. Optional: one per-person cap per run as the Trust feature.
A continuous video stream to every housemate. Send 2 to 4 frames per second plus item-added events through Firebase or Supabase. Real WebRTC is a build sink that judges won't notice.
Any leaderboard, feed, history or social profile.
verdicts.prior_art: TikTok Shop, Whatnot and Facebook Live already offer tap-to-buy from a live stream, but the stream there is run by the merchant, not by a friend's physical cart. Verishop Shop Party did shopping with friends over video, and Instacart's shopper photo chat already shows remote people what is in the cart. NeedAnything, Runerra and Buy4Me already let friends add items to your shopping run, which is what the reverse drag does. GrocerMate and Banana Split already match receipt lines to the people who asked for them, and Splitwise and Tab (a 2026 winner) already handle splitting and settling. Kando Errands gives each errand its own card but does not front money. What looks unclaimed, as far as these notes show: claiming one physical item from a friend's live cart by dragging it, with several people splitting the same item automatically, and each claim backed by a real card hold that is partially captured to that person's share at the actual receipt price, or voided if the item is never bought.
verdicts.best: The auto-split is the hero, and it is what the user asked for. At the table, a teammate's phone films a basket. Two judges each hold a phone with the feed and both drag the same eggs. The chip's ring splits in two, and each judge's screen shows a real Cybersource hold for the full $6 with 'you pay $3 at handoff'. At checkout, Perceptron reads the receipt ($5.49), and each judge's hold is partially captured at $2.75 while the unused hold is released. Two people at the table act within 10 seconds, the people present are where the money comes from, and the card events (hold, partial capture, void) are real and each one is needed. The build fits 4 people: (1) the shopper's camera with item-added detection and label OCR into chips, (2) a shared cart through realtime sync with drag-to-claim and the split math, (3) a Cybersource sandbox backend for hold, partial capture and void, and (4) receipt OCR that sets the capture amounts, plus the demo props and script.

objections: The part the user is most excited about is the least new. When several friends drag the same item and it splits evenly on its own, that is the standard 'shared item' toggle in Tab, SplitNow, Splitwise itemize, Banana Split (Devpost) and D-SplitBill (Devpost). All of them let 2-3 people claim one line and divide it evenly. If the ring splitting in two is the hero shot, a judge who has used Tab will shrug. What I could not find anywhere is the timing and the money behind the claim. The claim happens before the item is bought, in a physical store. Each claim is a real auth hold rather than an IOU. And an item nobody claimed never gets bought (the put-back rule). Lead with 'claim before Jake pays, and he never fronts.' Treat the split ring as a detail.

Every piece already ships somewhere, so the novelty is the combination plus the physical setting, not a new mechanism. Uber Eats group orders (2022) already let each person pick and pay for their own items before checkout, with a per-person spending limit. That is your cap and your no-fronting promise, just online. Rapyd Split (Devpost) already authorizes every group member's card and captures only once all shares are in. Caper / Instacart smart carts (Wegmans pilot, July 2025) already use cameras to detect items as they drop into a cart. Bulkshare.ai (2025 iOS app) and Club Save already pitch splitting Costco bulk packs with neighbors and students, though they coordinate through chat and don't take holds. Be ready to say exactly which piece is yours: in-store, before purchase, the claim is a hold, and unclaimed items get put back.

The camera is the weakest link in the pitch. The fallback ('tap add item and photograph it') does the same job as cart-entry detection, so a sharp judge will ask why you need continuous vision. The 2 fps feed to housemates goes against your own lesson that nobody watches a cart feed. The money is also awkward on student cards: every claimer is held for the full price plus 15%. Three people on a $30 pack means about $103 held across their cards, and with low limits that can trip the cap or cause a decline during the demo.
cut: The 2 fps cart feed on the housemate screen. The chips are the product. Without the feed, the privacy story shrinks to 'we only see the item photo', there are no frames to delete, and one realtime pipe goes away.

Continuous detection of items entering the cart. Make adding an item one shutter tap by the shopper on each item. Perceptron still crops it and reads the name and price, but you drop the entry-detection model, the clip-on mount and the main failure risk. The money moment still follows from something physical the camera sees.
Incremental auth for the case where the receipt price beats the hold. With a 15% buffer it won't come up in the demo. Mention it in one sentence and don't build it.
The shopper's separate Claim button on Shopper Cam. The shopper should claim from the same chip strip as everyone else, which means one claim code path.
Fuzzy receipt matching with tap-to-fix as a general system. You only need to match about 3 known props. Hardcode or lightly fuzz those, and keep tap-to-fix as the only fallback.
Card entry on the Join screen during the demo. Have the judge phones pre-joined with test cards loaded. Building Join beyond scan-the-QR is wasted effort.

Holding each claimer for the full price. Instead, re-auth or void-and-reauth when the claimer count changes, or hold each person for price ÷ claimers + 15%. That makes the hold match the visible share and avoids huge stacked holds. If it's too complex, keep full-price holds but don't show the big hold number in the hero shot.
verdicts.prior_art: I found nothing that exactly matches the core: people claiming the same physical item before purchase, each claim backed by a real card hold, an even split among claimers, and unclaimed items put back. That is why it isn't killed. The neighbors are close on every side. (1) Splitting one item evenly among people who claim it, after purchase: Tab, SplitNow, Splitwise itemize, Splyt (host still fronts), and Devpost's Banana Split and D-SplitBill. (2) Each person picks and pays for their own items before the order goes out, with a per-person spend limit: Uber Eats group order pay-your-own (CNBC, Mar 2022) and Uber for Business group ordering. That one is online and for restaurants. (3) Authorize everyone's card, capture later: Rapyd Split (Devpost) and the Adyen split-at-capture docs. (4) A camera that detects items going into a cart: Caper Cart / Instacart (Wegmans pilot July 2025), Amazon Dash Cart. (5) Splitting Costco bulk packs with neighbors or students: Bulkshare.ai (iOS, 2025, AI listing from a photo, chat-coordinated payments, only about 2 ratings) and Club Save / BulkBuySplitter. (6) Shared online carts: CartMates (Shopify), GroupKart. What's new is the combination: a physical store, a claim before the buy, the claim as a hold, and 'only buy what's claimed'. Sources: https://www.cnbc.com/2022/03/09/uber-eats-now-lets-everyone-pay-for-their-own-food-in-a-group-order.html , https://devpost.com/software/rapyd-split , https://devpost.com/software/banana-split , https://devpost.com/software/d-splitbill , https://apps.apple.com/us/app/-/id6752217571 , https://apps.apple.com/app/id1588691756 , https://investors.instacart.com/news-releases/news-release-details/instacart-and-wegmans-launch-pilot-caper-carts-enhance-store , https://apps.apple.com/app/id1605675055 , https://apps.shopify.com/cartmates
verdicts.best: The put-back rule plus holds. Jake only buys what someone has claimed, and every claim is already a hold on that person's card. That pairing is the one thing no receipt splitter, group-order app or bulk-share app does. It turns 'I'll Venmo you' into money already secured before the item reaches the register. It also gives Costco a real story: a bulk pack goes into the basket because two people claimed it. Put that in the first 10 seconds, ahead of the ring splitting.

objections: Every claim puts a separate hold on my card. On a 25-item Costco run that's 25 pending charges in my bank app, each at 115% of the full price, even when I'm only paying a third. Most of us use debit cards. Three of us claiming $26 paper towels means each card gets held $29.90, so my $60 checking balance gets tied up or declined over things I'm splitting, and I have to stare at ghost pendings for days. Fix: one hold per person per run, raised with incremental auth as I claim things, then one partial capture at settle. That's simpler to build and much less annoying to use.

Dragging every chip by hand gets old fast, and the put-back rule makes the shopper's job worse, not better. My housemates are in lecture, not watching chips. When Jake hits Checkout, half the cart is unclaimed, and now he's walking a 10 lb bag of rice back to aisle 40 because Priya didn't open her phone. In real life he just buys it, so the 'never stuck with it' promise breaks right away. Paper towels and dish soap are always split four ways in our house, and nobody wants to drag them every week. The multi-drag auto-split is the good part. The friction is having to claim every single item.

Clipping a phone over a Costco cart is the clunkiest piece. Costco packs often have no price sticker, the flatbed cart is huge, the stuff gets stacked, and the shopper has to drop items in one at a time so detection can keep up. Next to that, our current fix is good enough: Jake fronts $80 and posts the receipt to Splitwise. What actually hurts is chasing the money for weeks, and the hold-then-capture solves that. The camera mostly makes the demo look good; it doesn't help me.
cut: Per-item auth holds and per-item voids. Replace them with one Cybersource hold per person per run, using incremental auth as claims add up, and capture each person's exact total at settle. That's fewer API calls and less to debug, it removes the separate 'incremental auth edge case', and it fixes the statement clutter.

The separate per-run cap setting and its server-side mandate check. The run hold is the cap: when a claim would push you past it, the incremental auth gets refused. You keep the 'Over your $15 cap' demo beat without building a second system.

The 2 fps cart frame feed to housemates. Housemates need chips with photos, not a cart cam. Cutting it removes frame sync from the backend, the privacy surface on viewer phones, and a whole screen region. The camera stays on the shopper's phone only.
The 15% buffer math shown as 'Hold $X · your share ~$Y' on every chip. Show only 'your share ~$Y' on chips and the single run hold in the header.
The shopper's separate Claim button. The shopper is just another member with the same Mine tray.

Mandatory put-back. Unclaimed items go to the shopper by default and show as 'Jake's', with a gentle put-back nudge. That's one less forced action in the store. If the team loves the rice beat, keep it as a nudge only.
Talking about the merchant-of-record and Visa Direct licensing details at the table, beyond one sentence. Say 'payout simulated' and move on.
verdicts.prior_art: Splitwise (receipt scanning and itemized splits after purchase), Tab and Banana Split / GrocerMate (match receipt lines to people afterward), Venmo Groups (2024, shared expense groups), Instacart and Amazon Household shared carts (household members add items before purchase, but one payer fronts), Kando Errands (per-errand card), NeedAnything / Runerra / Buy4Me (friends request items on your run). None of these does what Dibs does: several people claim the same physical item before checkout, each claim backed by a pre-auth hold that is partially captured at the receipt price. The gap is real but narrow. Instacart shared carts come closest on the 'claim before buy' half.
verdicts.best: This is the feature the user asked for. Two judges drag the same egg chip, the ring visibly splits in two, and later each card is partially captured for exactly half the receipt price. The shopper never fronts money and never sends a Venmo request. It's a physical action with an instant, honest money consequence, and judges can do it in the first 10 seconds. The pain it solves is chasing a roommate for $23 for three weeks, and that is the one thing I'd actually switch apps for, as long as it costs me one hold per run instead of twenty.

objections: The promise is that the shopper never fronts money, but the step that pays the shopper back is the one you simulate. A Visa judge will also ask whether you tried the Visa Direct sandbox on the Visa Developer Platform, which offers push-funds (OCT) test calls with mutual-TLS credentials. Spend the first 2 hours trying to get those credentials. If you get them, the payout is real and this objection goes away. If you don't, say 'we tried, and here's the error' rather than 'not available to us'. A small terminology fix too: in Cybersource, releasing an uncaptured auth is an 'auth reversal'. 'Void' is for captures. A Visa judge will notice.

The hold design is more complicated than the demo needs. Every chip gets its own hold at the full label price plus 15%, for every claimer. Three people on a $30 pack means $103 in holds on three student debit cards, plus one statement line per chip. The spending cap is a check in your own server, not something Visa enforces. A simpler design: at Join, put one hold on each person for exactly their cap. Claims draw down from it with no API call. At settle, do one partial capture per person and reverse the rest. If someone raises their cap mid-run, use incremental auth, which gives it a real job. With this, 'Over your $15 cap' is enforced by the actual authorization, so the trust line becomes 'your cap isn't a setting, it's a hold.' You use 3 Visa calls, all of them necessary, and they're easier to explain in 15 seconds.

There's no agent, and the AI is mostly OCR. Technical Execution (20%) is carried by detecting items going into the cart and reading stickers and receipts. Of these, detection is the fragile part. In a top-down view at 2 frames per second, with hands over the basket and stickers facing down, the hero moment is the most likely thing to fail in front of a judge. Make the trigger deliberate: the shopper holds the item up to the lens for about 1 second, and Perceptron grounds it, crops it and reads the label. Put the AI credit where it's genuinely hard. Have Perceptron match Costco receipt shorthand ('KS EGGS 24CT') to the chip crops, and show its confidence on screen. Don't claim 'the camera sees it go in.'
cut: The 2-frames-per-second cart feed to housemates. The chip, with its cropped picture, name and price, is all a claimer needs. Cutting it removes a realtime frame pipeline, the 'frames deleted at run end' promise, and most of the privacy questions. The Cart Feed screen becomes just the chip strip plus the Mine tray.

Auto-detecting the 'item entering the cart' event. Replace it with holding the item up to the camera, keeping 'add item' as the fallback. This keeps the physical-to-money link and drops the riskiest vision job.
Separate holds per chip with a 15% buffer on each. Replace them with one cap-sized hold per person, made at Join.

Incremental auth for receipt prices above the hold. This edge case is never demoed, and incremental auth is finicky in Cybersource (the first auth has to be flagged as an estimate). Keep incremental auth only for raising your cap.

The put-back list and the shopper's Claim button. Requiring the shopper to claim their own groceries is friction that only exists to set up the rice beat. Default unclaimed items to the shopper. The drag-out reversal already shows money being released.
The detailed Settle breakdown of the buffer released on each hold. Show one line per person: paid share, rest released, with the auth ID.
Merchant-of-record and licensing detail on screen. Keep it to one sentence you say out loud if a judge asks.
Any mention of the Gemini browser shell during the pitch.
The 'nobody watches a cart feed' argument. Once the feed is gone, it isn't needed.
verdicts.prior_art: Splitting after the purchase is crowded: Splitwise itemized receipts, Tab, Splid, GrocerMate and Banana Split. Splitting at the moment of purchase also exists. As I recall, Cino (YC 2022) gave a group a shared virtual card and charged each member's own card their share when the purchase went through. I didn't verify this here, so check before the expo. Either way, at-purchase splitting isn't new, so don't claim it. Shared carts exist too (Instacart family carts, Amazon Household), but they are online and have no per-item claims. TikTok Shop, Whatnot and Shop Party are merchant-run carts. As far as I can tell, what hasn't shipped is several people claiming the same physical item before checkout, each claim backed by a real auth, settled by partial capture against the scanned receipt. Pitch only that narrow difference.
verdicts.best: Your own idea is the moment that wins the table. Both judges drag the same Kirkland eggs chip within seconds, a ring around it splits in two, and both phones show a real sandbox auth ID with 'your share ~$4.00'. Then the receipt scan turns that into $4.00 and $3.99 partial captures. A judge's finger causes a real Visa event in under 10 seconds, it's multiplayer with the people standing right there, and it needs no explanation. Spend all the build effort making that one gesture rock solid.

objections: The gesture you want to lead with, several friends claiming the same item and having it split automatically, has already been built for exactly this story. Devpost 'EasySplit' (devpost.com/software/easysplit) came from roommate Costco runs: photograph the receipt, Gemini extracts the lines, a QR code shares a live list, and friends pick items, with several people allowed on one item. Tab has offered 'multiple people can select the same item' since 2013. If a judge has seen any receipt splitter, the drag-and-split beat looks like a copy. The only new parts are timing and money: the claim happens before purchase, from an item held up to a camera, and a real auth hold backs it, partially captured against the receipt. Open on that, not on the split ring.

The pre-purchase money flow has close neighbors, so say 'new combination', not 'new primitive'. Cino (Balderton seed, not YC, so fix the spec) splits a card payment at the moment of purchase on a shared virtual Visa, but with preset ratios and not per item. Devpost 'Rapyd Split' charges no one until everyone has authorized their share, but only at online checkout. Uber Eats and DoorDash group orders already offer pay-your-own with a per-person limit. Bulkshare.ai splits Costco packs among neighbors through chat. What's unclaimed: a physical in-store item becomes a claimable chip, and each claim draws down a real per-person hold. That's narrow, so defend it precisely.

The payout to Jake, which is the 'he never fronts' promise in the opening line, is the part most likely to stay simulated, and it's also the regulatory weak spot. The app charges housemates as merchant of record and then pays Jake, which is money transmission. A Visa judge will see that the real Cybersource calls show money coming in but not reaching the person who was promised it. A two-hour Visa Direct mTLS attempt by the only backend engineer, on top of three other backend jobs, will probably fail and cost the realtime layer two hours.

Bulkshare.ai (split Costco packs with neighbors, AI listing from a photo, chat coordination, no holds). Walmart and Splitkart checkout splits (merchant side). I found no product or Devpost project where an item physically held up in a store becomes a live chip that remote friends claim before purchase, backed by a per-person auth hold and settled by partial capture against the scanned receipt. verdicts.best: 'Your cap isn't a setting, it's the hold itself.' Nobody in lecture is watching a chip strip live, and Jake is not going to stand in a Costco aisle holding up 25 items one at a time and waiting for drags. Your own spec admits real Costco packs have no price sticker, so the hold-up step depends on a prop that doesn't exist in the store.

verdicts.prior_art: I'd assume a judge has seen most of this. Tab and Splitwise already do itemized receipt scans with shared-item even splits. Bulkshare.ai splits Costco packs among people. Each person has one real Cybersource pre-auth, it's partially captured to exactly their receipt share, and the remainder is released, so no one ever chases a Venmo and the app can't take more than you approved. Pair that with the moment you asked about, several friends dragging the same chip and watching the ring auto-split, which is a fun hands-on judge interaction. objections: The main commerce moment can't happen with the numbers in the spec. Each judge has a $20 cap, and the eggs use about $4 of it, so each has about $16 left.
